sentences.text: Good morning. You have five stories today. Answers to your follow-up questions come first, and I'll start with the big news.
Our first big story is about Nvidia pausing chip shipments in Southeast Asia.
Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia.
Nvidia is checking whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements, and the pause has no set end date.
The reason is that Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers in the region.
The Institute for Progress estimates these remote data centers supply about 24% of China's AI computing power.
Now, a few stories picked for you, starting with a new approach to AI agent memory.
A new system called Leto treats memory as a prediction problem. It judges memory by how useful it is for future responses, not how faithfully it records the past.
On the PrefEval test, Leto beats the strongest rival memory system by 16.3 percentage points in accuracy.
On long multi-step tasks, it posts the best overall results, and its lead grows with chain depth.
Our next pick is about small modular nuclear reactors gaining ground in the United States.
At the end of September, the Tennessee Valley Authority became the first U.S. power utility authorized to build a commercial small modular reactor.
That project will use the GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 reactor. Only two SMR designs are approved for use in the United States so far.
Next, a practical lesson on why AI memory can give wrong answers.
Both the old and new seat preferences looked current, and nothing said which one should win.
Last, a story that is further from your usual reading.
OpenAI claims to have proved that omega, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4.
Another OpenAI release reportedly improves the known bound on the linear gates needed for the Fourier Transform.
What would you like to dig into?
